source.version: Working paper, The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, dated January 27, 2024 (SSRN 4708466 per search record; the document itself shows no SSRN number)
source.title_on_document: Prompting Diverse Ideas: Increasing AI Idea Variance

paper_design_summary: The authors prompt GPT-4 with 35 prompting strategies (base prompt, personas, creativity articles, emotional appeals, hybrid brainstorming, similarity information, Chain-of-Thought) to generate pools of product ideas for college students priced under USD 50, mostly 10 pools of 100 ideas per strategy. They score each pool's diversity by average pairwise cosine similarity (Google Universal Sentence Encoder) and compare it with a pool of 100 ideas written by Wharton MBA students, reused from Girotra et al. (2023). A second analysis generates about 1,200 ideas in one session with the base prompt and with Chain-of-Thought to estimate the number of unique ideas and the speed of exhaustion. No person in this paper receives AI help, and no new human participants are recruited.

studies.label: GPT-4 prompting strategies vs. pooled MBA-student ideas (cosine similarity, unique ideas, exhaustion)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No people were assigned. Prompting strategies were applied to GPT-4; the human comparison pool is an existing set of student ideas.
assignment.quote: As a baseline for comparison, we use a pool consisting of 100 randomly chosen ideas generated by Wharton MBA students. This is the same pool of ideas used as in Girotra et al 2023.
assignment.locator: p. 5, Prompting Strategies for Innovation and Brainstorming

participants.who: No participants recruited. The human comparison is a pool of 100 randomly chosen ideas by Wharton MBA students from Girotra et al. (2023), aggregated from multiple students; the number of students is not stated.
participants.quote: students were not tasked with generating 100 ideas at once, but instead the pool is an aggregation of ideas from multiple students.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 (gpt4-0314; gpt4-1106-preview for Chain-of-Thought and the exhaustion analysis), temperature 0.7, top P 1.0
ai_tool.how_used: Model generates idea pools on its own under 35 prompting strategies; no human uses the model.

task.description: New physical consumer product ideas targeted at US college students, retail price under about USD 50, 40-80 word paragraphs.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Girotra, Meincke, Terwiesch, and Ulrich (2023), 'Ideas are dimes a dozen' (SSRN 4526071): the 100 human ideas are the same Wharton MBA student pool; the Girotra et al. baseline and seeded GPT-4 pools also appear in Table 2.
sample_overlap.quote: This is the same pool of ideas used as in Girotra et al 2023.

eligibility.reason: No people are assigned to AI assistance and no participants are recruited. The paper compares diversity of GPT-4 idea pools across prompts and against an existing pool of 100 MBA-student ideas (Girotra et al. 2023), so it is AI-versus-human context evidence; most of the analysis is model-only prompt comparison. Criterion 3 is not met because no participant output is produced with or without AI.

one_line_finding: Within-pool cosine similarity is 0.243 for the student pool versus 0.255 for Chain-of-Thought prompting and 0.377 for the base GPT-4 prompt (range 0.255 to 0.432 across GPT-4 strategies), and Chain-of-Thought raises the estimated number of unique ideas from about 3,700 to about 4,700 (p. 3; Table 2, p. 11; p. 13).
open_questions: Design class could be read as model_only, since 35 of the comparisons are prompt-versus-prompt with no human output; I coded ai_vs_human because H1 and the headline result compare GPT-4 pools with the human idea pool.
notes: Outcomes left empty because none answers with_ai, across_people, or after_ai. For reference: outcome measures are (1) average within-pool cosine similarity, Google Universal Sentence Encoder, each strategy run 10 times (10x100 ideas) and averaged (p. 8-9; Table 2, p. 11; Figure 2, p. 10); (2) estimated number of unique ideas using a 0.8 similarity threshold and Kornish-Ulrich mark-recapture equation (p. 8; Appendix F, p. 37-38): base about 3,700 with 13.8 percent repetitive, CoT about 4,700 with 11.7 percent (p. 13); (3) speed of exhaustion, Figure 3, p. 13, difference persists up to about 750 ideas (p. 12); (4) between-pool similarity heatmap, Figure 4, p. 14. Significance: bootstrapping and permutation tests with p-values below 0.01, treating ideas as observations (p. 9). About 15 percent of CoT runs removed in the exhaustion analysis because the model skipped step two (p. 12). Appendix D (p. 20-36) lists a 'Lowest Cosine Add' pool at 0.144 built programmatically. Hybrid brainstorming simulates 40 GPT-4 'participants', not people (p. 5).
